But Paul applies to the Gentiles what was expressly spoken to the Israelites.<div eID="gen114869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114871" type="x-p"/>They who have hitherto been most successful in untying this knot have supposed that Paul meant to adopt this kind of reasoning, — “What may seem to be an hinderance to the Gentiles to become partakers of salvation did also exist as to the Jewish nation: as then God did formerly receive into favor the Jews, whom he had cast away and exterminated, so also now he exercises the same kindness towards the Gentiles.” But as this interpretation, though it may be supported, yet seems to me to be somewhat strained, let the readers consider this, — Whether it would not be a more suitable view to regard the consolation given by the prophet, as intended, not only for the Jews, but also for the Gentiles: for it was not a new or an unusual thing with the prophets, after having pronounced on the Jews God’s vengeance on account of their sins, to turn themselves to the kingdom of Christ, which was to be propagated through the whole world. And this they did, not without reason; for since the Jews so provoked God’s wrath by their sins, that they deserved to be rejected by him, no hope of salvation remained, except they turned to Christ, through whom the covenant of grace was to be restored: and as it was based on him, so it was then renewed, when he interposed. And doubtless, as Christ was the only refuge in great extremities, no solid comfort could have been brought to miserable sinners, and such as saw God’s wrath impending over them, except by setting Christ before their eyes, it was usual with the prophets, as we have reminded you, after having humbled the people by pronouncing on them divine vengeance, to call their attention to Christ, as the only true asylum of those in despair. And where the kingdom of Christ is erected there also is raised up that celestial Jerusalem, into which citizens from all parts of the world assemble. And this is what is chiefly included in the present prophecy: for when the Jews were banished from God’s family, they were thus reduced to a common class, and put on a level with the Gentiles. The difference being taken away, God’s mercy is now indiscriminately extended to all the Gentiles. We hence see that the prophet’s prediction is fitly applied to the present subject; in which God declares, that after having equalized the Jews and the Gentiles, he would gather a Church for himself from aliens, so that they who were not a people would begin to be so.<div eID="gen114871" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114868" osisID="Rom.9.25" type="section"/>
entries.02f8dc0457dc8a7566921946d5d122df95e2e427: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.26" sID="gen114872" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114873" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">I will call them my people which are not a people</hi> This is said with respect to the divorce, which God had already made with the people, by depriving them of all honor, so that they did not excel other nations. Though they indeed, whom God in his eternal counsel has destined as sons to himself, are perpetually his sons, yet Scripture in many parts counts none to be God’s children but those the election of whom has been proved by their calling: and hence he teaches us not to judge, much less to decide, respecting God’s election, except as far as it manifests itself by its own evidences. Thus Paul, after having shown to the Ephesians that their election and adoption had been determined by God before the creation of the world, shortly after declares, that they were once alienated from God, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.12">Ephesians 2:12</reference>,) that is, during that time when the Lord had not manifested his love towards them; though he had embraced them in his eternal mercy. Hence, in this passage, they are said not to be beloved, to whom God declares wrath rather than love: for until adoption reconciles men to God, we know that his wrath abides on them.<div eID="gen114873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114874" type="x-p"/>The feminine gender of the participle depends on the context of the prophet; for he had said, that a daughter had been born to him, to whom he gave this name,<hi type="italic"> Not beloved,</hi> in order that the people might know that they were hated by God. Now as rejection was the reason for hatred, so the beginning of love, as the prophet teaches, is, when God adopts those who had been for a time strangers. <note n="311"> <div sID="gen114875" type="x-p"/> The quotation is from <reference osisRef="Bible:Hos.2.23">Hosea 2:23</reference>, and is not literal either from the Hebrew or from the <hi type="italic">Septuagint. </hi>The order of the verse is reversed; and the word “beloved” is taken from the <hi type="italic">Septuagint. </hi>“Not beloved,” in Hebrew, is <hi type="italic">lo-ruhamah,</hi> <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>one not pitied, or one who has not received mercy: which is the same in meaning.<div eID="gen114875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114876" type="x-p"/>In <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.26">Romans 9:26</reference>, the words are taken from <reference osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.10">Hosea 1:10</reference> and are not <hi type="italic">verbatim </hi>either from the Hebrew or the <hi type="italic">Septuagint, </hi>but the difference is very trifling. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114876" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen114874" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114872" osisID="Rom.9.26" type="section"/>
entries.890dcc5afa0c906e935a101a4d630092ca993761: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.27" sID="gen114877" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27. </hi><hi type="italic">And Isaiah exclaims, etc.</hi> He proceeds now to the second part, with which he was unwilling to begin, lest he should too much exasperate their minds. And it is not without a wise contrivance, that he adduces Isaiah as exclaiming, not, speaking, in order that he might excite more attention. But the words of the Prophet were evidently intended to keep the Jews from glorying too much in the flesh: for it was a thing dreadful to be heard, that of so large a multitude, a small number only would obtain salvation. For though the Prophet, after having described the devastation of the people, lest the faithful should think that the covenant of God was wholly abolished, gave some remaining hope of favor; yet he confined it to a few. But as the Prophet predicted of his own time, let us see how could Paul rightly apply this to his purpose. It must be in this sense, — When the Lord resolved to deliver his people from the Babylonian captivity, his purpose was, that this benefit of deliverance should come only to a very few of that vast multitude; which might have been said to be the remnant of that destruction, when compared with the great number which he suffered to perish in exile. Now that temporal restoration was typical of the real renovation of the Church of God; yea, it was only its commencement. What therefore happened then, is to be now much more completely fulfilled as the very progress and completion of that deliverance.<div eID="gen114878" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114877" osisID="Rom.9.27" type="section"/>
entries.b49e2c90f9d84651732e8a803a36c7d589697796: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.28" sID="gen114879" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">For I will finish and shorten the matter, etc. </hi> <note n="312"> <div sID="gen114881" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Sermonem enim consummans et abbrevians</foreign>,” etc.; Λόγον γὰρ, etc. It is literally the <hi type="italic">Septuagint </hi>except in two instances: Paul puts in γὰρ, and substitutes ἐπὶ τὢς γὢς for ἐν τὣ οἰκουμένὟ ὅλὟ. It is a difficult passage in Hebrew: but the following rendering will make it materially consistent with the words of the Apostle, who evidently did not intend to give the words literally.<div eID="gen114881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114882" type="x-p"/>A destruction, soon executed, <lb/> <hi type="italic">Shall </hi>overflow in righteousness; <lb/> For completed and soon executed shall it be; <lb/> The Lord, Jehovah of hosts, shall do <hi type="italic">it, <lb/> </hi>In the midst of the whole land.<div eID="gen114882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114883" type="x-p"/>The word rendered above “soon executed,” means literally, abbreviated or cut short, signifying the quick execution of a thing or work. <hi type="italic">“Shall </hi>overflow in righteousness,” imports, “<hi type="italic">shall</hi> justly or deservedly overflow.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114883" type="x-p"/> </note> Omitting various interpretations, I will state what appears to me to be the real meaning: The Lord will so cut short, and cut off his people, that the residue may seem as it were a consumption, that is, may have the appearance and the vestige of a very great ruin. However, the few who shall remain from the consumption shall be a proof of the work of God’s righteousness, or, what I prefer, shall serve to testify the righteousness of God throughout the world. As <hi type="italic">word </hi>often in Scripture means a thing, the consummated word is put for consumption. Many interpreters have here been grossly mistaken, who have attempted to philosophize with too much refinement; for they have imagined, that the doctrine of the gospel is thus called, because it is, when the ceremonies are cut off, a brief compendium of the law; though the word means on the contrary a consumption. <note n="313"> <div sID="gen114884" type="x-p"/> There are many venerable names in favour of this opinion, such as <name>Ambrose</name><hi type="italic">, </hi><name>Chrysostom</name><hi type="italic">, </hi><name>Augustine</name><hi type="italic">, </hi>etc. Not knowing the Hebrew language, they attached a classical meaning to the expression, λόγον συντετμημένον, wholly at variance with what the Hebrew means, as <name>Calvin</name> justly observes. The word, συντετμημένον, in this passage, as <name>Schleusner</name> says, bears a meaning different from what it has in the classics; it imports what is cut short, that is, quickly executed. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114884" type="x-p"/> </note> And not only here is an error committed by the translator, but also in <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.22 Bible:Isa.10.23">Isaiah 10:22, 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.22">Isaiah 28:22</reference>; and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.11.13">Ezekiel 11:13</reference>; where it is said, “Ah! ah! Lord God! wilt thou make a completion of the remnant of Israel<hi type="italic">?” </hi>But the Prophets meant to say, “Wilt thou destroy the very remnant with utter destruction?<hi type="italic">” </hi>And this has happened through the ambiguity of the Hebrew word. For as the word, <foreign xml:lang="he">כלה</foreign><hi type="italic">, cale, </hi>means to finish and to perfect, as well as to consume, this difference has not been sufficiently observed according to the passages in which it occurs.<div eID="gen114880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114885" type="x-p"/>But Isaiah has not in this instance adopted one word only, but has put down two words, <hi type="italic">consumption, </hi>and <hi type="italic">termination, </hi>or cutting off; so that the affectation of Hebraism in the Greek translator was singularly unseasonable; for to what purpose was it to involve a sentence, in itself clear, in an obscure and figurative language? It may be further added, that Isaiah speaks here hyperbolically; for by consumption he means diminution, such as is wont to be after a remarkable slaughter.<div eID="gen114885" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114879" osisID="Rom.9.28" type="section"/>
entries.44a8901631c58bfd08b75dd3c27a47f9cd0c4e02:
29. And as Isaiah had before said, etc.
Isaiah 1:9. The words of the Septuagint are given literally, and differ only in one instance from the Hebrew; “seed” is put for “remnant;” but as “seed” in this case evidently means a small portion reserved for sowing, the idea of the original is conveyed. Schleusner refers to examples both in Josephus and Plato, in which the word “seed,” is used in the sense of a small reserved portion. Its most common meaning in Scripture is posterity.
Paul has given “Sabaoth” from the Septuagint, which is the Hebrew untranslated. This word, in connection with God, is variously rendered by the Septuagint: for the most part in Isaiah, and in some other places, it is found untranslated as here; but in the Psalms and in other books, it is often rendered τῶν δυναμέων, that is, Jehovah or Lord “of the powers,” and often παντοκράτωρ, “omnipotent;” and sometimes ὁ ἃγιος “the holy one.” But our version, “Jehovah” or “Lord of hosts,” is the proper rendering. It means the hosts of animate and inanimate creatures; in fact, the whole universe, all created things; but, according to the context, it often specifically refers to material things, or to things immaterial. — Ed.
He brings another testimony from the first chapter, where the Prophet deplores the devastation of Israel in his time: and as this had happened once, it was no new thing. The people of Israel had indeed no pre-eminence, except what they had derived from their ancestors; who had yet been in such a manner treated, that the Prophet complained that they had been so afflicted, that they were not far from having been destroyed, as Sodom and Gomorrah had been. There was, however, this difference, that a few were preserved for a seed, to raise up the name, that they might not wholly perish, and be consigned to eternal oblivion. For it behoved God to be ever mindful of his promise, so as to manifest his mercy in the midst of the severest judgments.
Romans 9:30-33
30. What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith.
30. Quid ergo dicemus? Quod gentes quae non sectabantur justitiam, adeptae sunt justitiam, justi-tiam autem ex fide:
31. But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness.
31. Israel autem sectando legem justitiae, ad legem justitiae non per-venit.
32. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;
32. Quare? Quid non ex fide, sed quasi ex operibus; offenderunt enim ad lapidem offensionis:
33. As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.
33. Quemadmodum scriptum eat, Ecce pono in Sion lapidem offensionis et petram offendiculi: et omnis qui crediderit in eum non pudefiet.
entries.f365a6a4041d8336fb338d050b53cda87e2323ab: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.30" sID="gen114900" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">What then, etc. </hi>That he might cut off from the Jews every occasion of murmuring against God, he now begins to show those causes, which may be comprehended by human minds, why the Jewish nation had been rejected. But they do what is absurd and invert all order, who strive to assign and set up causes above the secret predestination of God, which he has previously taught us is to be counted as the first cause. But as this is superior to all other causes, so the corruption and wickedness of the ungodly afford a reason and an occasion for the judgments of God: and as he was engaged on a difficult point, he introduced a question, and, as though he were in doubt, asked what might be said on the subject.<div eID="gen114901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114902" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That the Gentiles who did not pursue, etc.</hi> Nothing appeared more unreasonable, or less befitting, than that the Gentiles, who, having no concern for righteousness, rolled themselves in the lasciviousness of their flesh, should be called to partake of salvation, and to obtain righteousness; and that, on the other hand, the Jews, who assiduously laboured in the works of the law, should be excluded from the reward of righteousness. Paul brings forward this, which was so singular a paradox, in such a manner, that by adding a reason he softens whatever asperity there might be in it; for he says, that the righteousness which the Gentiles attained was by faith; and that it hence depends on the Lord’s mercy, and not on man’s own worthiness; and that a zeal for the law, by which the Jews were actuated, was absurd; for they sought to be justified by works, and thus laboured for what no man could attain to; and still further, they stumbled at Christ, through whom alone a way is open to the attainment of righteousness.<div eID="gen114902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114903" type="x-p"/>But in the first clause it was the Apostle’s object to exalt the grace of God alone, that no other reason might be sought for in the calling of the Gentiles but this, — that he deigned to embrace them when unworthy of his favor.<div eID="gen114903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114904" type="x-p"/>He speaks expressly of righteousness, without which there can be no salvation: but by saying that the righteousness of the Gentiles proceeded from faith, he intimates, that it was based on a gratuitous reconciliation; for if any one imagines that they, were justified, because they had by faith obtained the Spirit of regeneration, he departs far from the meaning of Paul; it would not indeed have been true, that they had attained what they sought not, except God had freely embraced them while they were straying and wandering, and had offered them righteousness, for which, being unknown, they could have had no desire. It must also be observed, that the Gentiles could not have obtained righteousness by faith, except God had anticipated their faith by his grace; for they followed it when they first by faith aspired to righteousness; and so faith itself is a portion of his favor.<div eID="gen114904" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114900" osisID="Rom.9.30" type="section"/>
entries.135f5de25c7eb0da1f907ac4bb13faad0d8e2725: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.31" sID="gen114905" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">But Israel, by pursuing, etc. </hi>Paul openly states what seemed incredible, — that it was no wonder that the Jews gained nothing by sedulously following after righteousness; for by running out of the way, they wearied themselves in vain. But in the first place it seems to me that the law of righteousness is here an instance of transposition, and means the righteousness of the law; <note n="315"> <div sID="gen114907" type="x-p"/> There seems to be no necessity for this transposition. “A law (not the law) of righteousness” means a law which prescribes righteousness, and which, if done, would have conferred righteousness. But the Jews following this did not attain to a law of righteousness, such a law as secured righteousness. The Apostle often uses the same words in the same verse in a different sense, and leaves the meaning to be made out by the context. <name>Grotius</name> takes “law” as meaning way, “They followed the way of righteousness, but did not attain to a way of righteousness.”<div eID="gen114907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114908" type="x-p"/>What follows the question in the next verse stands more connected with <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.30">Romans 9:30</reference> than with <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.31">Romans 9:31</reference>; and we must consider that the word righteousness, and not law, is referred to by “it” after the verb “pursue,” which is evidently to be understood before the words, “not by faith,” etc., as the sentence is clearly elliptical.<div eID="gen114908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114909" type="x-p"/>The verb διώκω, rendered “<foreign xml:lang="la">sector</foreign>“ by <name>Calvin</name><hi type="italic">, </hi>means strictly to pursue what flees away from us, whether a wild beast or an enemy; it signifies also to follow a leader, and to run a race, and further, to desire, to attend to, or <hi type="italic">earnestly </hi>to seek a thing: and in this latter sense Paul often uses it. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.13 Bible:Rom.14.19 Bible:1Cor.14.1">Romans 12:13; Romans 14:19; 1 Corinthians 14:1</reference>. Similar is the application of the corresponding verb, <foreign xml:lang="he">רדף</foreign> in Hebrew. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.20 Bible:Ps.34.14">Deuteronomy 16:20; Psalm 34:14</reference> <hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Quaero</hi></foreign> — <hi type="italic">to </hi>seek,” is the word adopted by <name>Grotius</name><div eID="gen114909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114910" type="x-p"/>But <name>Pareus</name> and <name>Hammond</name> consider that there are here three agonistic terms, διώκων κατέλαβε, and ἔφθασε. The first signifies the running; the third, the reaching of the goal; and the second, the laying hold on the prize: and with this corresponds the stumbling afterwards mentioned. The Gentiles did not run at all, but the Jews did, and in running, they stumbled; while the Gentiles reached the goal, not by running, or by their own efforts, but by faith, and laid hold on the prize of righteousness. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114910" type="x-p"/> </note> and then, that when repeated in the second clause, it is to be taken in another sense, as signifying the model or the rule of righteousness.<div eID="gen114906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114911" type="x-p"/>The meaning then is, — “That Israel, depending on the righteousness of the law, even that which is prescribed in the law, did not understand the true method of justification.” But there is a striking contrast in the expression, when he teaches us that the legal righteousness was the cause that they had fallen away from the law of righteousness.<div eID="gen114911" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114905" osisID="Rom.9.31" type="section"/>
entries.2cc9fc9968ec73bbf02ca59b7678610688ea622d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.9.32" sID="gen114912" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32. </hi><hi type="italic">Not by faith, but as it were by works, etc.</hi> As false zeal seems commonly to be justly excused, Paul shows that they are deservedly rejected, who attempt to attain salvation by trusting in their own works; for they, as far as they can, abolish faith, without which no salvation can be expected. Hence, were they to gain their object, such a success would be the annihilation of true righteousness. You farther see how faith and the merits of works are contrasted, as things altogether contrary to each other. As then trust in works is the chief hinderance, by which our way to obtain righteousness is closed up, it is necessary that we should wholly renounce it in order that we may depend on God’s goodness alone. This example of the Jews ought indeed justly to terrify all those who strive to obtain the kingdom of God by works. Nor does he understand by the works of the law, ceremonial observances, as it has been before shown, but the merits of those works to which faith is opposed, which looks, as I may say, with both eyes on the mercy of God alone, without casting one glance on any worthiness of its own.<div eID="gen114913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114914" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For they have stumbled at the stone, etc.</hi> He confirms by a strong reason the preceding sentence. There is indeed nothing more inconsistent than that they should obtain righteousness who strive to destroy it. Christ has been given to us for righteousness, whosoever obtrudes on God the righteousness of works, attempts to rob him of his own office. And hence it appears that whenever men, under the empty pretence of being zealous for righteousness, put confidence in their works, they do in their furious madness carry on war with God himself.<div eID="gen114914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114915" type="x-p"/>But how they stumble at Christ, who trust in their works, it is not difficult to understand; for except we own ourselves to be sinners, void and destitute of any righteousness of our own, we obscure the dignity of Christ, which consists in this, that to us all he is light, life, resurrection, righteousness, and healing. But how is he all these things, except that he illuminates the blind, restores the lost, quickens the dead, raises up those who are reduced to nothing, cleanses those who are full of filth, cures and heals those infected with diseases? Nay, when we claim for ourselves any righteousness we in a manner contend with the power of Christ; for his office is no less to beat down all the pride of the flesh, than to relieve and comfort those who labour and are wearied under their burden.<div eID="gen114915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114916" type="x-p"/>The quotation is rightly made; for God in that passage declares that he would be to the people of Judah and of Israel for a rock of offence, at which they should stumble and fall. Since Christ is that God who spoke by the Prophets, it is no wonder that this also should be fulfilled in him. And by calling Christ the <hi type="italic">stone of stumbling, </hi>he reminds us that it is not to be wondered at if they made no progress in the way of righteousness, who through their wilful stubbornness stumbled at the rock of offence, when God had showed to them the way so plainly. <note n="316"> <div sID="gen114917" type="x-p"/> “Error is often a greater obstacle to the salvation of men than carelessness or vice... Let no man think error in doctrine a slight practical evil. No road to perdition has ever been more thronged than that of false doctrine. Error is a shield over the conscience and a bandage over the eyes.” — <hi type="italic">Professor </hi><name>Hodge</name><div eID="gen114917" type="x-p"/> </note> But we must observe, that this stumbling does not properly belong to Christ viewed in himself; but, on the contrary, it is what happens through the wickedness of men, according to what immediately follows.<div eID="gen114916" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.9.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114912" osisID="Rom.9.32" type="section"/>
entries.b968d75344f4760a31ea93f241a50574e58e9840:
33. And every one who believes in him shall not be ashamed. He subjoins this testimony from another part for the consolation of the godly; as though he had said, “Because Christ is called the stone of stumbling, there is no reason that we should dread him, or entertain fear instead of confidence; for he is appointed for ruin to the unbelieving, but for life and resurrection to the godly.” As then the former prophecy, concerning the stumbling and offence, is fulfilled in the rebellious and unbelieving, so there is another which is intended for the godly, and that is, that he is a firm stone, precious, a corner-stone, most firmly fixed, and whosoever builds on it shall never fall. By putting shall not be ashamed instead of shall not hasten or fall, he has followed the Greek Translator. It is indeed certain that the Lord in that passage intended to strengthen the hope of His people: and when the Lord bids us to entertain good hope, it hence follows that we cannot be ashamed.
The citation in this verse is made in a remarkable manner. The first part, “Behold I lay in Zion,” is taken from Isaiah 28:16; what follows, “a stone of stumbling and rock of offense,” is taken from Isaiah 8:14; and then the last words, “and whosoever believes in him shall not be ashamed,” are given from the preceding passage in Isaiah 28:16. The subject is the same.
With respect to the last clause Paul has followed the Septuagint, “shall not be ashamed.” But the Hebrew word, rendered in our version “shall not make haste,” will bear a similar meaning, and may be translated, shall not hurry or be confounded. — Ed.
See a passage like this in 1 Peter 2:10
CHAPTER 10
Romans 10:1-4
1. Brethren, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
1. Fratres, benevolentia certe cordis mei, et deprecatio ad Deum super Israel, est in salutem.
2. For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
2. Testimonium enim reddo illis, quod zelum Dei habent, sed non secundum scientiam:
3. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
3. Ignorantes enim Dei justitiam, et propriam justitiam quaerentes statuere, justitiae Dei subjecti non fuerunt;
4. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
4. Finis enim Legis Christus in justitiam omni credenti.
The γὰρ, “for,” at the beginning of Romans 10:4, connects it with the latter part of the preceding, as the γὰρ, “for,” in the preceding connects it with the latter part of Romans 10:2; and γὰρ also in Romans 10:5 expresses a reason for what Romans 10:4 contains. So that we have a regular chain; the following sentence gives a reason for the one immediately preceding in four instances. — Ed.

But then still the dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficulty is, <ns0:hi>How,</ns0:hi> and in what Sence the Apostle wisht him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self <ns0:hi>accursed</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>separated from Christ.</ns0:hi> The received Opini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on is, That out of Zeal to the <ns0:hi>Glory of God,</ns0:hi> and Love to his <ns0:hi>Brethren</ns0:hi>; he was willing to be <ns0:hi>damned,</ns0:hi> that they all might be <ns0:hi>saved.</ns0:hi> Many of the Ancients did thus Expound this place. <ns0:hi>Christ become a curse for us; And what Marvel is it</ns0:hi> (sayes one) <ns0:hi>if the Lord would be made a</ns0:hi> curse <ns0:hi>for the Servants, that a Servant should be willing to become an</ns0:hi> Ana<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thema <ns0:hi>for the Brethren. He doth not wish</ns0:hi> (sayes another) <ns0:hi>for his</ns0:hi> brethrens sake, <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> Separated from the love and grace of Christ, <ns0:hi>but from the</ns0:hi> comforts <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> Christ, <ns0:hi>and the future</ns0:hi> happiness <ns0:hi>that we have by him: He is content to lose his part in the heavenly Glory, if that might promote the</ns0:hi> Glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of Christ, <ns0:hi>which would be more Illustrated by the saving a whole Nation, than a particular Person,</ns0:hi> q. d. <ns0:hi>If this might be the Fruit of it, if it would to this end, I could methinks be content to part with all my</ns0:hi> hopes in Christ, <ns0:hi>even my e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal Happiness, upon condition my Brethren might be Parta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kers thereof; so Passionate, and abundant Love have I to and for them.</ns0:hi> This Exposition is not Satisfactory. Therefore some think, the Apostle here speaks of being <ns0:hi>accurst</ns0:hi> only for a Season, or of being an <ns0:hi>Anathema</ns0:hi> in this World. An <ns0:hi>Anathema</ns0:hi> sometimes signifieth Corporal Death and De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction; of old, in times of common Calamity, they were wont to Sacrifice Men to their <ns0:hi>Idols,</ns0:hi> and infernal gods, for the pacifying of their Anger: Such a Sacrifice they cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>Anathema,</ns0:hi> which is a word here used, <ns0:hi>q. d. For my Brethrens sake, that so they might be Saved; I could be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tent to be cut off, to be made a Sacrifice, to Dye the worst of Deaths.</ns0:hi> But if this be admitted, How then is that Clause to be understood (<ns0:hi>from Christ?</ns0:hi>) 'Tis not, I could wish my self an <ns0:hi>Anathema,</ns0:hi> but an <ns0:hi>Anathema from Christ</ns0:hi>; to this, they Answer that favour this Interpretation; that instead of <ns0:hi>from Christ,</ns0:hi> you may read <ns0:hi>by Christ.</ns0:hi> q. d. <ns0:hi>I could be content to be cut off or destroyed by Christ, that my Brethren might be saved.</ns0:hi> This Sence of the words suits well with the Zeal and Kindness of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> to his <ns0:hi>Brethren, Exod.</ns0:hi> 32.32. rather than they should not be pardoned and Spared, he prays, <ns0:hi>That God would blot him out of the book that he had written, vid. Annot.</ns0:hi> there. There is yet another, and a more probable Interpretation of this <ns0:hi>Wish</ns0:hi> of the Apostle. 'Tis as if he had said, I could be willing to be Separated or Excommunicated from the <ns0:hi>Church of Christ,</ns0:hi> for the Sake and Salvation of my <ns0:hi>Country</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Nation. Anathema</ns0:hi> (sayes he <ns0:hi>Hesychius</ns0:hi>) signifies <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Excommunicate, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.22. <ns0:hi>If any Man love not the Lord Iesus Christ, let him be Anathema:</ns0:hi> Let him be removed from the Christian As<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />semblies; deprived of those Christian Priviledges that are afforded there, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Let him be an Anathema,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>teacheth another Gospel, i. e.</ns0:hi> Turned out of the <ns0:hi>Church of Christ,</ns0:hi> and avoided by all true Christians; If this Sence be admitted, then <ns0:hi>(from Christ)</ns0:hi> must signify <ns0:hi>from the body of Christ</ns0:hi>; and so the word <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> is used, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.12. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.27. <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> being the <ns0:hi>Head</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Body</ns0:hi>; he that is cut off from the <ns0:hi>body,</ns0:hi> may be truly enough said, to be cut off <ns0:hi>from Christ.</ns0:hi> Thus the Apostle <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> who was Accu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed and Persecuted by the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> for having made a De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection from the <ns0:hi>Law of Moses,</ns0:hi> and setting up <ns0:hi>Christian Assemblys,</ns0:hi> in opposition to their <ns0:hi>Iudaical</ns0:hi> Service; doth fi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ly express his Kindness and Love to them, in wishing himself depraved of those most valuable Priviledges, on condition they might be Partakers thereof. To this it may be added, That in the Primitive Times, this <ns0:hi>Anathemati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zing</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Excommunicating,</ns0:hi> was attended with delivering up to Satan, and that with Destruction of the Flesh, with very sharp and severe Punishments upon the Bodyes of Men: And so <ns0:hi>Anathemae</ns0:hi> in this Notion, may be taken with this Improvement, and may contain all those Temporal Cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities, that he was willing to endure and undergo for their <ns0:hi>Good (vid.</ns0:hi> D. H. <ns0:hi>in Loc.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>, for my brethren, my kins<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men according to the flesh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">So the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi>

Isaac</ns0:hi> was Born of a Free-woman, and when <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>circumcised</ns0:hi>; but <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> was Born of a Bond-woman, and when <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>uncircumcised:</ns0:hi> Besides, <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> no sooner came to Years, but he shewed some Tokens of Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versness, and of a wicked Spirit. Therefore, in this, and the Three following Verses, he doth give another, which was beyond all Exception; and that is in <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> betwixt whom there was no Disparity, either in Birth or in Works: They had both one and the same Mother; <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />becca</ns0:hi> Conceived with them at one and the same time; and that by no other Person, than <ns0:hi>our Father Isaac</ns0:hi>; and yet the one of these is Chosen, and the other Refused. This now was an undeniable Proof, that the <ns0:hi>promise</ns0:hi> belongs not to all the Children of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> or of <ns0:hi>Isaac,</ns0:hi> according to the Flesh; All the <ns0:hi>Seed</ns0:hi> of neither are the Children of the <ns0:hi>promise.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11. (For <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> As there was nothing in the Birth of those Twins, so neither in their Works, that occasioned the Difference that God made bewixt them; For when God spake of what should happen to them, they were Unborn, and had done neither Good nor Evil.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>the children</ns0:hi> being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He means, <ns0:hi>Actual good or evil</ns0:hi>; such as might Difference them one from another. As for Original Sin, they were both alike tainted there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with.</ns0:note>, that the purpose of God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This Purpose of God is to be understood about <ns0:hi>Reprobation,</ns0:hi> or (if you will) <ns0:hi>Rejection,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Praeterition,</ns0:hi> as well as about <ns0:hi>Election.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> according to election might stand <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Be Firm or Stable.</ns0:note>, not of works <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either done or foreseen.</ns0:note>, but of him that calleth) <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the good Pleasure and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deserved <ns0:hi>Favour of God,</ns0:hi> who also effectually Calleth those that He Hath Elected, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8.30. See a Parallel place, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12. It was said unto her, The <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>greater.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> elder shall serve the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>lesser.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> younger <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This Verse is to be Read with the <ns0:hi>Tenth.</ns0:hi> The whole <ns0:hi>Eleventh</ns0:hi> Verse being a Parenthesis. Then when She re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sorted to the Lord for Counsel, about the Strugling of the Children in her Womb; it was told her, or revealed to her of God, that <ns0:hi>The Elder should serve the Younger:</ns0:hi> Of the Sence of which words, see <ns0:hi>Annot.</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25.23. where they are Recorded.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:423" />13. As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The foregoing Oracle is expounded by another taken out of <ns0:hi>Malachi.</ns0:hi> 1.2, 3. see the <ns0:hi>Annot.</ns0:hi> there. Because the foregoing passage of <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> his serving <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> doth not seem so full and clear, to betoken the Election of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and the Rejection of <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> in the purpose of God; therefore the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle brings this place to Explain the former; and proves that the service or subjection of <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> was accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />panied with Gods Eternal and undeserved <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> of the one, and his <ns0:hi>Iust</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Righteous hatred</ns0:hi> of the other. There are some, that by <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> do understand their Posterity, and not their Persons; that say, the <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hatred of God,</ns0:hi> in the forecited Text, doth only or chief<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly respect Temporal things; God <ns0:hi>loved Iacob, i. e.</ns0:hi> He gave him the <ns0:hi>Land of Promise</ns0:hi>; but <ns0:hi>hated Esau, i. e.</ns0:hi> He gave him a <ns0:hi>Dry</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Barren</ns0:hi> Country, and made his Mountain wast; That by <ns0:hi>Gods hating Esau,</ns0:hi> is only meant he <ns0:hi>Loved</ns0:hi> him less than <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> &c. Such should consider, That the scope of the Apostle is, to shew, That some are the <ns0:hi>Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of God,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>Promise,</ns0:hi> and not others; and they must not make him Cite Testimonys out of the <ns0:hi>Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment</ns0:hi> impertinently. Much is Written <ns0:hi>pro and con</ns0:hi> upon this Argument. But I remember, he that writes a Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mentary, must not too far involve himself in Controver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sy.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14. What shall we say then? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 32.4. 2 Chron. 19.7. Job 34.10.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>Is there</ns0:hi> unrighteousness with God? God forbid <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Another Anticipation of an Objection. Some might Object and say, if God Elect some, and Reject others, their case being the same, or their Persons being in themselves equal and alike, then he is Unjust and Partial: To this he Answers, 1. More generally, with his repeated Note of Detestation, <ns0:hi>God forbid</ns0:hi>; the <ns0:hi>Syriake</ns0:hi> Translator Reads it <ns0:hi>God forgive</ns0:hi>; Noteing thereby, the hainousness of such a thought, and then He Answers this Cavil more particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larly; shewing 1. That God is not unjust in <ns0:hi>Electing</ns0:hi> some, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15, 16. And 2. That he is not unjust in <ns0:hi>Rejecting</ns0:hi> others, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15. For he saith to Moses, I will have mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> God is not chargeable with any injustice in <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lecting</ns0:hi> some, and not others; for this is an Act of meer <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>compassion,</ns0:hi> and that can be no violation of Justice. To prove this, he cites a Testimony out of <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 33.19. <ns0:hi>vid. locum.</ns0:hi> There He tells <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> That the good Pleasure of His <ns0:hi>Will,</ns0:hi> was the only Rule of all his favourable and merciful Dealings with the Children of Men. The same thing is intended and expressed in Two several Phrases: And the Ingemination imports the Free<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of God's <ns0:hi>Mercy</ns0:hi>; nothing moves Him thereunto, but his own gracious Inclination; and also the Arbitrariness thereof; it depends only upon his good <ns0:hi>Will</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pleasure.</ns0:hi> The Sum is, if God shew <ns0:hi>Mercy</ns0:hi> to some, and not to others, He cannot be accused of injustice, because He injures none; nor is He obliged or indebted to any.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16. So then <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth mercy <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> God's <ns0:hi>Election</ns0:hi> is not of <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi>'s, or of any other Man's <ns0:hi>willing</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>running, i. e.</ns0:hi> It is not from his good De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sires or Deeds, his good Inclinations of Actions, or from the fore-sight thereof; but it is of God's meer <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>good pleasure.</ns0:hi> This Text wounds <ns0:hi>Pelagianism</ns0:hi> under the fifth Rib. <ns0:hi>Nec volenti, nec volanti,</ns0:hi> was the Motto of a No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Personage.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17. For the Scripture saith unto Pharaoh <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This Verse shews, That God is not unjust in <ns0:hi>Rejecting</ns0:hi> others of equal Condition with the <ns0:hi>Elect:</ns0:hi> For the Proof of which, he cites a Testimony out of <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 9.16. This Verse must be joyn'd with the 14. <ns0:hi>God forbid,</ns0:hi> for the Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture saith, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God saith in the Scripture.</ns0:note>, Even for this same purpose have I <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>raised thee.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> raised thee up <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. I have crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted or promoted thee to be King in Egypt.</ns0:hi> Or, (as some) <ns0:hi>I have raised</ns0:hi> or stirred <ns0:hi>thee up to oppress my People:</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>I have hardened thee,</ns0:hi> a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> it follows in the next Verse, <ns0:hi>and given thee up to thy own rebellious and obstinate Mind.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, that I might shew my power in thee <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> I have done what I have done for this very end, that the whole World may Ring of <ns0:hi>my Power and Glory.</ns0:hi> And this shews, that it is not unjust in God to <ns0:hi>reject Sinners</ns0:hi> of the Children of Men, because thereby he farthers his own Glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry. For this end <ns0:hi>all things</ns0:hi> are made, and all things are accordingly ordered and disposed, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 16.4.</ns0:note>, and that my name might be declared through<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out all the earth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18. <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>so <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Therefore] <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This Verse is a short Repetition of the fore-going Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument.</ns0:note> hath he mercy on whom he will <ns0:hi>have mercy</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. and the Notes there.</ns0:note>, and whom he will, he harde<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In a judicial way. Besides natural <ns0:hi>hardness,</ns0:hi> which is in all men, and is Hereditary to them; and habitual <ns0:hi>hardness,</ns0:hi> which is Contracted by a Custome in Sin. As a Path is <ns0:hi>hardened</ns0:hi> by the continual trampling of Passengers; there is judicial or ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diciary <ns0:hi>hardness,</ns0:hi> which is inflicted by God as a Punishment. Men <ns0:hi>harden</ns0:hi> their own hearts sinfully (so 'tis thrice said of <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Exodus,</ns0:hi> That <ns0:hi>He hardened his own heart, Exod.</ns0:hi> 8.15. and 9.34.) and then <ns0:hi>God hardens their hearts</ns0:hi> judi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially; so 'tis often said of God in <ns0:hi>Exodus,</ns0:hi> That <ns0:hi>He har<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dened Pharaoh</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>heart, Exod.</ns0:hi> 7.13. and 9.12. and 10.1, 20, 37. and 14.8. God is not said properly to <ns0:hi>harden the hearts of men, i. e.</ns0:hi> He doth not make their soft hearts hard, nor doth he put <ns0:hi>hardness</ns0:hi> into the <ns0:hi>hearts</ns0:hi> of Men (as our Adversaries slanderously report us to Affirm) nor doth he barely permit or suffer them to be <ns0:hi>hardened,</ns0:hi> (which is the Opinion of the <ns0:hi>Papists,</ns0:hi> about this matter;) but Two wayes may He be said to <ns0:hi>harden sinners.</ns0:hi> 1. By forsaking them, and not softning their <ns0:hi>Hearts</ns0:hi>; As <ns0:hi>darkness</ns0:hi> follows upon the <ns0:hi>Sun</ns0:hi>'s with-drawing of his <ns0:hi>light</ns0:hi>; so doth <ns0:hi>hard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s with-holding his <ns0:hi>softning</ns0:hi> Influence. 2. By Punishing them, He inflicts farther <ns0:hi>hardness,</ns0:hi> as a Punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of former <ns0:hi>hardness</ns0:hi>; and this he infuseth not; but it is Effected, Either 1. By Satan, to whom <ns0:hi>hardned sinners</ns0:hi> are delivered up: Or 2. By themselves, they being given over to their own <ns0:hi>hearts</ns0:hi> Lusts. Or 3. By <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>word</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>works,</ns0:hi> which accidentially <ns0:hi>harden</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>hearts</ns0:hi> of Men, as might be shewn.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19. Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Here he obviates a Third Objection or Cavil. The <ns0:hi>First</ns0:hi> was, That God is <ns0:hi>unfaithful, ver.</ns0:hi> 6. The <ns0:hi>Second,</ns0:hi> That God is <ns0:hi>unjust, ver.</ns0:hi> 14. Now the <ns0:hi>Third</ns0:hi> is, That God is <ns0:hi>se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vere</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>cruel.</ns0:hi> Some might object and say, If God, in those Courses which He takes with <ns0:hi>Men</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sinners,</ns0:hi> doth follow only his own <ns0:hi>will</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>pleasure</ns0:hi>; and all things are done thereafter. Why then doth He complain of Sinners<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and find Fault with them? It seems it is his <ns0:hi>will</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>reject</ns0:hi> them; and, Who hath Resisted, or can make Resistance there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />unto? It seems to be a common Saying amongst the <ns0:hi>Hebrews,</ns0:hi> That <ns0:hi>none can withstand God, vid.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20.6. <ns0:hi>(& alibi.)</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20. <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Here follows the Answer to this Cavil; which is ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Personal to the Caviller in this, and the next Verse, or real to the Cavil in the two following Verses.</ns0:note> Nay but, O man, who art thou that re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pliest <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>to Go<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> again, or <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putest with God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> against God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Apostle seems to speak these words with some warmth, as if his Spirit and Zeal was stirred at the sawciness of the Caviller. <ns0:hi>q. d. Dost thou consider what thou art?</ns0:hi> Thou art but a Man, a piece of living Clay, a little breathing Dust, a contemptible Worm in comparison; and darest thou to word it with <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> to dispute with thy <ns0:hi>Maker</ns0:hi>; to questi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on or call <ns0:hi>Him</ns0:hi> to an account? You may argue Matters with your fellow Creatures, but not with your <ns0:hi>Creator,</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 45.9, 10. from whence this seems to be borrowed, <ns0:hi>vid. Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 40.2.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 64.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Shall the thing for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med, say to him that formed <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> Why hast thou made me thus <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Shall the <ns0:hi>Wood</ns0:hi> quarrel with the <ns0:hi>Carpenter,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Iron</ns0:hi> with the <ns0:hi>Smith</ns0:hi>; or as 'tis in the next Verse, the <ns0:hi>Clay</ns0:hi> with the <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi>?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21. Hath not the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Je<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 18.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Tim. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He Argueth from the Less to the Greater, That if a <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> hath <ns0:hi>power over his Clay,</ns0:hi> to Form it as he plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seth, then <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> hath much more <ns0:hi>power</ns0:hi> over his <ns0:hi>Creatures,</ns0:hi> to Form them, or order them as He listeth. <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Autho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity</ns0:hi> over his <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi> is Greater, than that of a <ns0:hi>Power</ns0:hi> over his <ns0:hi>Clay.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> made not his <ns0:hi>Clay</ns0:hi>; but both <ns0:hi>Clay</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> are made by <ns0:hi>God.</ns0:hi> Here is something implied, that as there is no difference in the <ns0:hi>matter</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lump,</ns0:hi> out of which the <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> frameth diversity of <ns0:hi>Vessels:</ns0:hi> So there is no difference in Man-kind; all Men are alike by Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, and in the same <ns0:hi>corrupt State</ns0:hi>; both those who are <ns0:hi>Elected,</ns0:hi> and those who are <ns0:hi>Rejected,</ns0:hi> that are made <ns0:hi>vessels</ns0:hi> of mercy, or <ns0:hi>vessels</ns0:hi> or wrath. And here is this expressed, That as the <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> maketh <ns0:hi>vessels of honour</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>dishonour,</ns0:hi> of nobler or viler Use, out of <ns0:hi>the same lump,</ns0:hi> as he listeth; and is not bound to give a Reason of his so doing to his <ns0:hi>Pots.</ns0:hi> So God may <ns0:hi>chuse</ns0:hi> some, and <ns0:hi>reject</ns0:hi> others, and give no Account thereof unto his Creatures. The <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> takes nothing from the <ns0:hi>Clay,</ns0:hi> of what Form soever he makes it; and the <ns0:hi>Creator</ns0:hi> doth no Wrong to the Creature, however he doth dispose of it.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22. <ns0:hi>What</ns0:hi> if God, willing to shew <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much long-suffering the vessels of wrath <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> fitted to destruction <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> What hast thou to answer or object against God, if He take a severe Course with some? Seeing, 1. He there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by Manifesteth his great <ns0:hi>displeasure</ns0:hi> against <ns0:hi>Sin,</ns0:hi> and his <ns0:hi>Power</ns0:hi> to take Vengeance of <ns0:hi>Sinners:</ns0:hi> Seeing, 2. He bears long with them in their Sins; exerciseth great <ns0:hi>Patience</ns0:hi> towards them, in the midst of their Provocations; giving them space to Repent, if they can or will: And seeing, 3. They are <ns0:hi>Vessels of wrath,</ns0:hi> fitted to Destruction: Partly by themselves, and their own sensual Courses; Partly by <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Righteous Iudgment,</ns0:hi> who gives them up thereunto.</ns0:note>?<ns0:note place="bottom">In this, and the next Verse, is a real Answer to the Cavil, in <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19. The Apostle having spoken before of God's absolute <ns0:hi>Right</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Power</ns0:hi> over his Creatures, to dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose of them at his Pleasure, as the <ns0:hi>Potter</ns0:hi> doth his <ns0:hi>Clay.</ns0:hi> Lest any should tax <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> with Tyranny and Partiality to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards his Creatures, He sub-joyneth the Reasons of his different proceedings with the one, and with the other.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:423" />23. And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Again, on the other side, What hast thou to say, if he proceed more Mercifully with others? Seeing, 1. He thereby Manifesteth the <ns0:hi>Riches of his Glory,</ns0:hi> or his glorious Grace: And seeing, 2. They are <ns0:hi>Vessels of Mercy, which he had afore prepared unto Glory, i. e.</ns0:hi> He had done it by Electi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on from Eternity, and by Regeneration, and Sanctification of the Spirit in time. He speaks here of Two sorts of <ns0:hi>Vessels,</ns0:hi> some of <ns0:hi>wrath,</ns0:hi> and some of <ns0:hi>mercy,</ns0:hi> as he had before spoken of <ns0:hi>Vessels of honour,</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>dishonour:</ns0:hi> Concerning the Latter, he speaks Passively, That they are <ns0:hi>fitted to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction, vid. ver.</ns0:hi> 22. Concerning the Former, he speaks Actively, That God hath <ns0:hi>prepared</ns0:hi> them <ns0:hi>unto glory.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24. Even, us whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Hitherto he hath been shewing, That the <ns0:hi>Promise</ns0:hi> was never made or meant to the Carnal Seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi> This Argument he began <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 6, 7. and he continues it (using several Apostrophes and Amplifications, which were to his purpose) till he comes to these words; and here he tells you plainly, who are the True <ns0:hi>Seed of Abraham,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Children of the Promise</ns0:hi>; even the <ns0:hi>called of God</ns0:hi> of all <ns0:hi>Nations,</ns0:hi> whether <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gentiles.</ns0:hi> And he takes occasi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on to fall into it, by speaking of some in the foregoing Verse, that were <ns0:hi>Vessels of mercy afore prepared unto glory</ns0:hi>; Now here, in this Verse, he tells you who these are (and to be sure they are the Persons he is enquiring after, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Spiritual Seed of Abraham,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Children of the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise</ns0:hi>) He sayes, They are such as <ns0:hi>God called, i. e.</ns0:hi> Effectu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally <ns0:hi>called, not of the Iews only, but of the Gentiles also</ns0:hi>; and that this is so, he farther proves in the following Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25. As he saith also in Osee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.10.</ns0:note> I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her, Beloved, which was not beloved <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Here the Apostle proves, That the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> were <ns0:hi>chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of the promise,</ns0:hi> or that the <ns0:hi>promise</ns0:hi> belonged to them, as well as to the <ns0:hi>Iews:</ns0:hi> And because the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> could not endure to hear of this, he cites Two Testimonyes out of <ns0:hi>Hosea,</ns0:hi> to convince them: One is in this Verse, and it is taken out of <ns0:hi>Hosea</ns0:hi> 2.23. The other is in the following Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26. And it shall come to pass, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> in the place where it was said unto them, Ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not my people; there shall they be called, The children of the living God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This Testimony is taken out of <ns0:hi>Hosea</ns0:hi> 1.10. And 'tis as if he had said; This that I Affirm concerning the Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />version, and <ns0:hi>calling</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> is nothing else but what the Prophet <ns0:hi>Hosea</ns0:hi> long ago did Preach to our Fathers. Some think, these places in <ns0:hi>Hosea</ns0:hi> do speak <ns0:hi>primarily</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Iewes,</ns0:hi> and but <ns0:hi>secundarily,</ns0:hi> or by consequence of the <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles.</ns0:hi> Others think, that they speak chiefly of the <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles:</ns0:hi> Those Terms <ns0:hi>(not beloved, and not a people)</ns0:hi> being in Scripture mostly used of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27. Esaias also cryeth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Hereby is noted the Prophets Zeal, or his openness and plainness. The Testi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mony Recorded, is found in <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.22, 29.</ns0:note> concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">For Num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber or Multitude, for so the <ns0:hi>promise</ns0:hi> was to <ns0:hi>Abraham, Gen.</ns0:hi> 22.17. and 32.12.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note place="margin">C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 11.5.</ns0:note> a remnant shall be saved <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Shall return, i. e.</ns0:hi> From the Captivity, or from Sin (as 'tis <ns0:hi>Isai.</ns0:hi> 10.21.) This shews, none can be <ns0:hi>saved,</ns0:hi> but they which Return and Repent.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">In this, and the Two next Verses, he proves, That it was foretold of old, by <ns0:hi>Esaias</ns0:hi> the Prophet, That God should pass by the greatest part of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>save</ns0:hi> on<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly <ns0:hi>a remnant,</ns0:hi> or a few of them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28. For he will finish <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 paragraph">
                        <ns0:desc>〈1 paragraph〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> the work, and cut <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This Verse is also found in that forecited place, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.22, 23. The Apostle in this, and in the other Cita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, follows the <ns0:hi>Seventy,</ns0:hi> which was a received Transla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and had been in request about <ns0:hi>Three Hundred</ns0:hi> Years, though in this and in other Places, it is very different from the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text; That which God is said to <ns0:hi>finish,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>cut short is his work.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which signifies his <ns0:hi>word,</ns0:hi> or the Account, as some read it. This is brought in as a Reason, why a <ns0:hi>remnant</ns0:hi> only should be <ns0:hi>saved</ns0:hi>; be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause God would shorten the Account, or (as we read it) make <ns0:hi>a short work</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> world. He would bring a sudden Destruction upon that people. <ns0:hi>Senacherib,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Assyrians,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Titus Vespatian,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> shall make a compleat and speedy Conquest of them; Few of them shall remain, the greater part being involved; First in In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fidility, then in Destruction. The Apostle makes those <ns0:hi>few</ns0:hi> to be a <ns0:hi>Type of God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Elect</ns0:hi> among that People, that should be <ns0:hi>Saved by Faith</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Iesus Christ.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29. And as Esaias said before <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 1.9.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lam. 3.22.</ns0:note> Except the Lord of sabaoth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or of <ns0:hi>Hosts:</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Mighty God,</ns0:hi> whose <ns0:hi>Host</ns0:hi> all Creatures are, which Execute his <ns0:hi>Will,</ns0:hi> as Souldi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers the Will of their Commander.</ns0:note> had left us a seed <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He means by <ns0:hi>a Seed,</ns0:hi> the same that he meant before by <ns0:hi>a Remnant</ns0:hi>; a small num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber. These were left as a little <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> out of a great heap of Corn; that which is <ns0:hi>chosen,</ns0:hi> and left for <ns0:hi>Seed,</ns0:hi> is little in comparison of the whole Crop.</ns0:note>, we had been as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 13.19.</ns0:note> Sodoma, and been made like unto Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />morrha <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Utterly wasted and destroyed as they were, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50.40.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30. What shall we say then <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This is the Conclusion of the Apostles Discourse a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout the <ns0:hi>Election</ns0:hi> of some, and the <ns0:hi>Rejection</ns0:hi> of others; as also about the <ns0:hi>calling</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>casting</ns0:hi> off the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>? That the Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles which followed not after righteousness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That never minded or regarded it: Instead of following after it, they Fled from it. They were full of all Unrighteousness, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.18. to the end, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.2, 3.</ns0:note>, have attained to righteousness, even the righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness which is of faith <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz. Gospel-Righteousness,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Righteousness of Christ,</ns0:hi> which is received by <ns0:hi>true Faith.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31. But Israel <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.2. & 11.7.</ns0:note> which followed after the law of righteousness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The unbelieving <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who paid great Reverence to the <ns0:hi>Law of God,</ns0:hi> regarding and observing the outward Precepts and Ceremonies thereof.</ns0:note>, hath not attained to the law of righteousness <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They came short of that <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> which the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> requires, which God will Accept; and which is to be <ns0:hi>attained,</ns0:hi> not by <ns0:hi>works,</ns0:hi> but by <ns0:hi>faith,</ns0:hi> as it follows in the next Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32. Wherefore <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Here is the Reason of the foregoing seeming Paradox; why they, who followed after the <ns0:hi>Law of Righteousness,</ns0:hi> should not <ns0:hi>attain</ns0:hi> it, rather than other; <ns0:hi>because they sought it not</ns0:hi> aright; <ns0:hi>they sought it not</ns0:hi> in a way of Believing, but of Working: These Two are Opposed in the business of <ns0:hi>Iustification,</ns0:hi> as before at large, in <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 3. and 4.</ns0:note>? Because <ns0:hi>they sought it</ns0:hi> not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> As if they could <ns0:hi>have attained Righteousness</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iustification</ns0:hi> in that way, which was impossible to do.</ns0:note>: For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 2.34.</ns0:note> they stumbled at that stumbling-stone <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The true <ns0:hi>Messiah. q. d.</ns0:hi> So far were they from seeking <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> that on the contrary they took Offence at him, to their own Destruction, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 6.3. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.23. They thought it impossible that he should give them a <ns0:hi>Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> better than their own. This happened to them ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the Prophecy that went before them: So it followeth;</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33. As it is written <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8.14. and 28.16. to which Prophecy al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so, the Apostle <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> refers, in 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.6, 7, 8.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 21.42.</ns0:note> Behold I lay in Sion a stumbling stone <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iesus Christ</ns0:hi> is properly a <ns0:hi>Corner Stone,</ns0:hi> Elect and Precious; but accidentally and eventually a <ns0:hi>Stumbling Stone, Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.34.</ns0:note>, and rock of offence, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.11.</ns0:note> whosoever believeth on him, shall not be <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>confound<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shamed <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Or Confounded. <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>He that believeth</ns0:hi>; the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Whosoever believeth</ns0:hi>; which is much the same: An indefinite Proposition is equivalent to an Universal: The Prophet saith, <ns0:hi>He that believeth shall not make hast</ns0:hi>; the Apostle, <ns0:hi>He shall not be ashamed.</ns0:hi> He that is Rash and Hasty will at last be <ns0:hi>ashamed</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>confounded.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
            </ns0:div>
